About

Analytics in service of students & decisions

I’m a data analytics professional with 7+ years turning data into decisions across fintech, automotive data, government IT, consulting, and higher-education institutional research.

At UNCW’s Office of Institutional Research & Planning, I build institutional reports and dashboards, strengthen data quality, and partner with campus stakeholders — working day to day with SQL, Python, Tableau, and statistical analysis.

Alongside my role, I’m pursuing a Doctor of Information Technology at Trine University (4.0 GPA), where my interests sit at the intersection of data science, cybersecurity, and responsible, decision-ready analytics. I enjoy connecting with fellow data and analytics professionals — feel free to reach out.

Off the clock, I’m a traveler — I’ve lived in 12 cities across three countries, and I keep a map of all of it.

AI Radar · Daily Brief

What AI did today

AI is moving stupid fast, and nobody can keep up by scrolling all day — so I keep a radar. Here’s the short version: what’s new, what to watch out for, and what genuinely blew my mind. Every source competes on merit — the big labs, the startups, the open-source world, all of it.

ai-radar — daily brief / SAT · NOV 14, 2026 · EDITION 028 / The AI Radar — Saturday, November 14, 2026 FEED SYNCED LATEST BRIEF
TL;DR — THE 20-SECOND VERSION Your AI agent can now pay for purchases — with your approval on every single one — Meta’s agent will make the phone calls you keep putting off, a Google model just took the independent math crown, Gemini glasses are up for preorder, the engine behind local AI hit version 1.0, DeepSeek opened its app’s best tricks to developers, and one coordinator agent quietly beat every team of agents. Here is what actually matters, in plain words.
01PAYMENTSOPENAINOV 13, 2026

Your AI agent can now pay for things — with your fingerprint on every purchase

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on November 13. It lets the company’s always-on agents, called dots, complete purchases for you — but the agent never sees your real card number. The payment network swaps in a token instead, and you review the items, the total, and the card, then approve each purchase with Face ID or a fingerprint. It is built with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, and starts with ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US, aged 18 and up, with eligible US-issued cards.

WHY IT MATTERSWhy it matters: Agents just crossed from suggesting to spending. The guardrail is the honest part — a human approves every single purchase, at least for now.
SOURCE → REUTERS
02AGENTSMETANOV 12, 2026

Meta’s Muse will now make the phone calls you keep putting off

Meta opened Muse’s calling feature to all paid subscribers in the US this week, after testing it since September. Muse can call a cable company, an insurer, the DMV, or a restaurant that does not take online bookings — and it can sit on hold for you. Plans start at $20 a month, and Meta says Muse now has more than 10 million users. One honest catch from the reporting: some businesses hang up the moment they realize an AI is calling.

WHY IT MATTERSWhy it matters: This is the errand nobody wants, handed to an agent. Whether it works now depends less on the AI and more on whether the person who picks up stays on the line.
SOURCE → TECHCRUNCH
03MODELSGOOGLENOV 13, 2026

A Google model just took the math crown from OpenAI

Gemini 4 Carbon moved to No. 1 on MathArena, a third-party benchmark that tests models on fresh math competition and research problems they have not seen in training. The benchmark’s operator announced it on November 13: Carbon scored 85.4% overall, with Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 in second place. One caveat, stated plainly by the operator himself: because of cost, Carbon has not yet been run on every evaluation.

WHY IT MATTERSWhy it matters: Leaderboards flip all the time, but this one is run by an outsider, on unseen problems — and it is the first non-OpenAI model on top there in a very long time.
SOURCE → AI ORIENS
04WEARABLESGOOGLE · SAMSUNGNOV 12, 2026

Gemini glasses you can actually preorder — from $395

Google, Samsung, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster opened preorders for their first Gemini smartglasses, with sales starting December 10 in the US and South Korea. Warby Parker frames start at $395 and Gentle Monster at $449. There is no display in the lens — you talk to Gemini by voice, ask about what the 12-megapixel camera sees, get directions, or translate a conversation live. Google says they weigh about 41 grams and last up to nine hours on a charge.

WHY IT MATTERSWhy it matters: No screen, no gimmick — just an assistant you wear. If AI is going to live outside the phone, this simple version is the one most people would actually try.
SOURCE → AI DAILY DIGEST
05OPEN SOURCEGGML-ORGNOV 13, 2026

The engine behind local AI just turned 1.0 — and made a promise

llama.cpp and its ggml library reached version 1.0.0 on November 13, about three and a half years after the project started. These are the tools that let people run AI models on their own laptops and phones, and they now support more than 150 model architectures. The big news is a promise: from here on, anything that breaks compatibility arrives only in a major version release, so apps built on it will not break overnight. The release also removes 35 deprecated functions and adds FP8 KV caches.

WHY IT MATTERSWhy it matters: A lot of private, offline AI quietly runs on this project. A stable 1.0 means the local-AI world just got a firmer floor to build on.
SOURCE → AI NEWSWAY
06DEVELOPERSDEEPSEEKNOV 13, 2026

DeepSeek put its app’s best tricks into the API

DeepSeek opened the tools behind its consumer app to developers on November 13. Through its API, apps can now switch on web search, file and web-page reading, and safety checks inside a normal model call, with OCR and voice available as separate services. DeepSeek also released an open-source demo chat app under the MIT license, so anyone can see — and copy — how it all fits together.

WHY IT MATTERSWhy it matters: Features that used to take a whole stack of separate tools now come in one call. That lowers the bar for small teams building real, useful AI apps.
SOURCE → AI COMPASS
07RESEARCHANTHROPICNOV 11, 2026

One coordinator agent beat a whole team of agents — every time

Anthropic Fellows tested what happens when several people each send their own agent into a shared task — a team budget, a clinic calendar, a group order. In all four test setups, one coordinator agent serving everyone beat the team of personal agents, by about 10 to 45 percentage points; the personal agents stalled, overrode each other, and sometimes made things up. The team released three of the test worlds as an open benchmark called MAMUBench. It is simulated and still a preprint, so read it as a strong signal, not settled law.

WHY IT MATTERSWhy it matters: Everyone is rushing to give every person their own agent. This is early evidence that how agents share — or do not — matters more than how many you deploy.
SOURCE → ANTHROPIC ALIGNMENT
SIGN-OFFThat is today’s Radar. Agents learned to pay and to phone — and then the research reminded us they still work best with one coordinator in charge. See you tomorrow. — Akanksha

REEL 01 · HIGHER-ED ANALYTICS · IPEDS

Retention Beats Wealth

Nine years of federal data, 8,670 colleges — Pell students finish at 45.9%, their classmates at 62.2%. The strongest predictor of finishing? First-year retention.

REEL 02 · HIGHER-ED ANALYTICS · IPEDS

Everyone Rose. The Gap Stayed.

Seven entering classes, 2009–2015 — Pell students climbed from 38.9% to 45.9%, their classmates from 54.4% to 62.2%. The gap between them: 15.5 points at the start, 16.4 at the end.

Watch on Instagram ↗ Watch on LinkedIn ↗ Watch on YouTube ↗ Full analysis (GitHub) ↗
REEL 03 · HIGHER-ED ANALYTICS · IPEDS

16.4 Is the Headline. 7.7 Is the Campus.

The famous Pell gap is 16.4 points — but that counts every student in the country, so the biggest institutions pull it up. Count campuses instead, one vote each, and the typical campus gap is 7.7 points. At 16% of campuses, Pell students actually finish ahead.

Watch on Instagram ↗ Watch on LinkedIn ↗ Watch on YouTube ↗ Full analysis (GitHub) ↗
REEL 04 · AI MODELS · REAL EXPERIMENT

Easy vs Hard

I gave ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini the same two problems. On the easy-looking one, two of them counted a duplicated row and answered 1,765 instead of 1,637. On the hard-looking one, all three pooled the totals correctly — 83.63%.

Watch on Instagram ↗
REEL 05 · CYBERSECURITY · DEEPMIND

Old Locks

DeepMind’s AI agents found two new weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA. One forgery attack now runs up to 1,600 times faster, and factoring extra keys in a batch costs about 30 times less. Modern encryption is fine — the risk is the old systems still running it.

Watch on Instagram ↗ Watch on LinkedIn ↗ Watch on YouTube ↗ Watch on Facebook ↗
REEL 06 · AI AT WORK · ROCKY PRESENTS

Go Nuts

Cisco handed one engineer an unlimited AI budget and told him: go nuts. His job is to refactor 98% of Cisco’s legacy code in two years, with a team of two — and he is 27. The honest part: 98% is a target, not a result; he gets four weeks to prove the method works. Rocky presents.

Thirty Minutes

Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome 2 reads DNA cell by cell — and reproduced a bowel-disease finding in about 30 minutes that took a Francis Crick Institute team 18 months of lab work.
